title: Adolescence: puberty, risk taking and HEEADSSS assessment
blurb: Explain normal puberty, run a HEEADSSS psychosocial assessment in the right order, and balance a young person's confidentiality with safeguarding.
question: A 15-year-old is admitted with abdominal pain and her mother stays at the bedside. The nurse wants to complete a psychosocial assessment. How should it be set up and in what order should topics be explored?

teach.body: Adolescence is the move from childhood to adulthood: the body changes through puberty, and young people seek more independence, privacy and peer connection. Experimenting and taking some risks is part of this stage, so nurses screen for risks routinely and respectfully rather than waiting for a crisis. Plain English: treat the young person as the main person in the room, and ask about life, not just symptoms.

teach.caption: NHS 111 Wales: puberty; NHS: early or delayed puberty. Early or late puberty needs medical assessment.
Doukrou and Segal, Arch Dis Child Educ Pract 2018. Start with easier topics to build rapport.

teach.h: See the young person alone for part of it
teach.body: Offer all children and young people the chance to be seen separately from their parents for part of the consultation, and ask how involved they want their parents to be. Explain confidentiality and its limits BEFORE sensitive questions: what they say stays private unless there is a risk of serious harm to them or others, in which case you would need to share it.

steps.label: Time alone
steps.sub: Parent steps out for part of it

teach.caption: Fraser guidelines cover contraception and sexual health advice. Always encourage involving parents.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Kayla on the adolescent ward
items: Kayla, 15, is admitted with abdominal pain. Nurse Jo explains she talks to all young people about their wider life and asks Kayla's mother to step out for a few minutes.
Jo explains confidentiality and its limits, then works from Home and Education through Eating and Activities before Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide and Safety.
Kayla says she has a boyfriend aged 21 who buys her alcohol and has asked her to 'help a friend' carry parcels.
Jo recognises possible exploitation, explains she must share this to keep Kayla safe, and follows the safeguarding procedure.

teach.text: Do not open with the most sensitive questions, and do not promise total secrecy. Order is Home first, Safety last; confidentiality is explained with its limits before you start.

items.label: start transition planning by age 13-14 at the latest (NG43)
consent to treatment as effective as an adult's (FLRA 1969 s8)
sexual activity: always a child protection referral

items: Puberty usually starts 8-13 in girls (breast budding first) and 9-14 in boys (testicular enlargement first).
HEEADSSS: Home, Education, Eating, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide, Safety; least to most sensitive.
Offer time alone; explain confidentiality and its limits first.
Share to safeguard when there is risk of serious harm, abuse or exploitation.
Plan transition to adult services from Year 9 at the latest.

summary: You can now describe normal puberty, carry out a HEEADSSS assessment in the right order with time alone and a clear explanation of confidentiality, and recognise when a disclosure must be shared to safeguard the young person.

A.q: Ethan, 14, attends clinic with his mother. The nurse wants to complete a psychosocial assessment. What is the most appropriate way to begin?
options: Ask his mother to answer questions on his behalf
Ask Ethan about drug use while his mother is present
Offer to see Ethan alone for part of the consultation
Give Ethan a questionnaire to complete at home
A.why: NICE NG204 advises offering young people time separately from their parents for part of the consultation, which allows a more open HEEADSSS conversation.

whyNot.0: The young person is the main source; parents answering for him limits his voice.
whyNot.1: Sensitive topics should come later, after rapport and confidentiality are explained, and are better explored privately.
whyNot.3: A questionnaire at home misses the chance for a supported, confidential conversation.

A.q: What does HEEADSSS stand for in the UK form used for adolescent psychosocial assessment?
options: Home, Education, Eating, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide, Safety
Health, Education, Exercise, Alcohol, Diet, Sleep, Stress, Smoking
Home, Exercise, Eating, Anxiety, Drugs, Sleep, School, Safety
Health, Emotions, Eating, Activities, Diet, Sexuality, Self-harm, Sleep
A.why: HEEADSSS: Home, Education/employment, Eating, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide/depression, Safety (Doukrou and Segal 2018).

whyNot.1: This mixes lifestyle topics; it is not the HEEADSSS framework.
whyNot.2: Exercise, Anxiety, Sleep and School are not the letters of HEEADSSS.
whyNot.3: Health, Emotions, Diet, Self-harm and Sleep are not the HEEADSSS headings.

A.q: Chloe, 10, has started breast development. Her father asks if this is too early. What is the most accurate reply?
options: It is early, as puberty usually starts at 13
It is early, as puberty usually starts at 12
It is late, as puberty usually starts at 8
It is within the normal range of 8 to 13 years
A.why: Puberty in girls normally starts between 8 and 13 years, with breast budding usually the first sign.

whyNot.0: 13 is the upper end of the normal range, not the usual start.
whyNot.1: The average start for girls is about 11, and 10 is well within the normal range.
whyNot.2: 8 is the lower end of the normal range; starting at 10 is not late.

B.q: A nurse is about to ask Aisha, 15, the more personal HEEADSSS questions. What should she do first?
options: Promise that everything said will stay secret
Explain confidentiality and when it would be shared
Ask her mother's permission to ask about sex
Tell Aisha her answers will be passed to her GP
B.why: Explaining confidentiality and its limits before sensitive questions lets the young person decide what to share, knowing serious risks would be shared to keep them safe.

whyNot.0: Total secrecy cannot be promised because risks of serious harm must be shared.
whyNot.2: A young person's sexual health can be discussed confidentially; parental permission is not required to ask.
whyNot.3: Routine sharing of everything with the GP is inaccurate and would discourage honesty.

B.q: During a HEEADSSS assessment, Leah, 12, says she is having sex with a boy of 15. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Give confidential contraception advice as Fraser applies
Record it and discuss at her next appointment
Ask her to tell her parents herself this week
Follow safeguarding procedures and share the concern
B.why: Sexual activity involving a child under 13 should always result in a child protection referral, and safeguarding information must be shared.

whyNot.0: Fraser guidelines do not apply to a child under 13; this is a child protection matter.
whyNot.1: Delay is unsafe; a referral is needed now.
whyNot.2: Encouraging her to tell parents does not meet the duty to safeguard her.

B.q: Why does HEEADSSS start with Home and Education rather than Drugs or Sexuality?
options: Easier topics first build rapport before sensitive ones
Home and school are the topics parents care most about
Drug and sexual questions are for doctors to ask
The order follows how common each risk is
B.why: HEEADSSS is asked from least to most sensitive, building rapport and trust before harder topics.

whyNot.1: The order is about the young person's comfort, not parental priorities.
whyNot.3: The sequence is by sensitivity, not prevalence.

C.q: Callum, 15, has type 1 diabetes and two DKA admissions this year. He used to manage well. His parents say he now skips insulin and stays out late. What is the best initial nursing approach?
options: Tell Callum he must let his parents give his insulin
Arrange an urgent transfer to adult diabetes services
Explore his life with a HEEADSSS assessment, seen alone
Ask his parents to supervise every injection
C.why: A change in self-care in adolescence calls for understanding the wider picture (home, school, peers, mood, drugs, safety) in a confidential conversation before planning support.

whyNot.0: Removing his control without understanding the cause can worsen engagement.
whyNot.1: Transition is planned from Year 9 and is not a response to a crisis.
whyNot.3: Taking over supervision before understanding the cause ignores his developmental need for independence.

C.q: Mia, 14, tells the nurse during a HEEADSSS assessment that her 22-year-old boyfriend buys her alcohol and has asked her to carry packages for his friends. What should the nurse do?
options: Keep it confidential as Mia has asked
Explain it must be shared and follow safeguarding
Give advice on alcohol and safer relationships
Ask Mia's mother whether she knows him
C.why: These are indicators of possible sexual and criminal exploitation. Confidentiality has limits: the nurse should explain she must share this and follow safeguarding procedures (s16LA).

whyNot.0: Risk of serious harm and exploitation overrides a request for confidentiality.
whyNot.2: Advice alone does not address the safeguarding risk.
whyNot.3: Questioning the parent first may alert the alleged exploiter and delays the referral.

C.q: Ryan, 16, says during a psychosocial assessment that lately he feels nothing is worth it. Which HEEADSSS area does this fall under and what is the next step?
options: Suicide/depression: ask directly about suicidal thoughts
Activities: encourage him to join a sports club
Education: ask his school to monitor his mood
Safety: advise him on road and online safety
C.why: Feeling that nothing is worth it falls under Suicide/depression; the nurse should ask directly and sensitively about thoughts of self-harm or suicide and act on the answer.

whyNot.1: Activities may help later, but the risk needs exploring first.
whyNot.2: Passing the concern to school does not assess his immediate safety.
whyNot.3: Safety in HEEADSSS covers injuries and exposure to violence, not this mood disclosure.

reteach.title: Climb the ladder
reteach.question: Why would you not ask a teenager about sex in your first question?

blocks.h: From safe ground to sensitive ground
blocks.body: Think of HEEADSSS as a ladder. Home, school and food are the low rungs: easy to talk about. Drugs, sex, mood and safety are higher rungs. Climb in order, with the parent out of the room and confidentiality explained, and the young person is far more likely to tell you what is really going on.

blocks.text: Confidential does not mean secret. Explain the limits before you start.

explain.body: Girls: usually 8-13 years, average about 11, first sign breast budding; signs before 8 are early. Boys: usually 9-14, average about 12, first sign testicular enlargement; signs before 9 are early.

test.q: What is usually the first sign of puberty in boys?
options: Voice breaking and deepening
Facial and body hair growth
A growth spurt in height
Testicular enlargement
test.why: Testicular enlargement is usually the first sign of puberty in boys.

whyNot.0: The voice breaks later in puberty.
whyNot.2: The growth spurt in boys tends to come after puberty has begun.

explain.body: Home, Education/employment, Eating, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide/depression, Safety: least to most sensitive.

test.q: Which HEEADSSS topic is usually explored first?
options: Drugs
Sexuality
Home
Safety
test.why: Home is the first, least sensitive topic.

whyNot.0: Drugs come after Home, Education, Eating and Activities.
whyNot.1: Sexuality is one of the more sensitive topics, later in the sequence.

explain.body: Offer to see the young person without their parents for part of the consultation (NG204). Explain that you keep what they say private unless there is a risk of serious harm, when you would need to share it.

test.q: What does NICE NG204 advise about involving parents in consultations with young people?
options: Parents should be present for the whole consultation
Offer time alone and ask how involved they want parents
Parents should leave for the whole consultation
Ask parents to decide how involved they will be
test.why: NG204 1.5.2: ask young people how involved they want their parents to be and offer to see them separately for part of the consultation.

whyNot.0: This removes the chance to speak privately.
whyNot.2: Parents are usually involved for part of the consultation, as the young person wishes.
whyNot.3: The young person's preference guides parental involvement.

explain.body: Sexual activity under 13, abuse, exploitation or serious risk of harm must be shared to safeguard the young person. Tell them you are doing so, unless that would increase risk.

test.q: Which disclosure from a 15-year-old must be shared to safeguard them?
options: Being pressured to carry drugs for an older man
Feeling stressed about forthcoming exams
Having a 15-year-old girlfriend
Wanting to try a vegetarian diet
test.why: Being coerced to carry drugs by an older person is an indicator of child criminal exploitation and must be shared.

whyNot.1: Exam stress needs support but is not a safeguarding disclosure on its own.
whyNot.2: A relationship with a peer of the same age is not on its own a safeguarding concern.
whyNot.3: A diet choice is not a safeguarding issue; eating is explored in HEEADSSS for other reasons.
